findings.passage: Four leads because the pattern she describes in the present tense, withdrawal into longing and then into song, is the Four's.
findings.problem: The verdict says Four leads because withdrawal is her present-tense pattern and helping is her past. The sources the draft cites say otherwise. (1) In the July 2026 Z100 interview (S19, about 13:00-15:00), "if you don't want me, don't have me" is her rejection of withdrawal, not her withdrawal. She describes her old stance as "I'm not going to start a relationship... I'm not getting into another friendship cuz it's going to end", then gives the new one: "So be it. Allow it to end. Like if you don't want me, don't have me." She adds "you can allow something to matter without trying to make it permanent" and "I'm a very loyal and I can be very valuable to some people." (2) The Zach Sang "completely opposed to being in a relationship" line (S13, about 04:00) is also past tense: "I was completely opposed... I became very closed off and became very sad. And it's not the way to live." (3) In the same Zach Sang interview (about 49:00) she describes giving in the present tense: "I always feel like I give a lot of myself... So if I love somebody I'll do anything... that's how I've lived," and says it has been "taken advantage of." (4) In the March 2026 Z100 interview (S18) she says she has been the helper "for ages" and calls it "the biggest theme throughout my whole life." What she says she learned "recently" to stop was clinging ("hold on so tight... or be too much"), not being of service. The article repeats the misreading in four places: 'Making herself needed' ('the helper is who she used to be'; 'What she describes now runs the other way'), the Type 2 subsection ('is not how a Two usually protects a relationship'), the Four case ('when she expects to lose someone now, she withdraws instead of giving more'), and the Type 2 FAQ ('she tells that story in the past tense, and by July 2026 her stance on relationships had become...'). This is a context-fidelity error, and the leading read's stated tie-breaker depends on it.
findings.acceptance_test: Wherever the article uses "if you don't want me, don't have me," it is presented in her framing: accepting that things end and declining to close herself off, with "Allow it to end" or equivalent context. No sentence in the body or FAQs calls her current stance withdrawal or says the helper role is only in her past, unless an opened, dated source supports it. The verdict sentence and the Type 2 FAQ either give a reason for the leading read that survives these four passages, or say that tense does not separate Four from Two. If the leading type changes as a result, the run follows the standard's --refresh --expanded-review path.

findings.passage: The song holds the record's clearest Four lines.
findings.problem: The draft takes Four evidence from "Pure" (the sister-envy lyric, "I wish I was real," the applause story) and leaves out what she says the song is mainly about. In the Cosmopolitan answer the draft quotes (S36, about 01:00), the first lyric she names as "very very personal" is a line about her mother's pain and wanting to feel what her mother felt. Only then does she mention the sister lyric. In the iHeartRadio answer the draft cites for "was very depressed at the time" (S17, about 06:00-07:00), the same sentence goes on to say her mother was ill at home in London while she was writing in LA, and that "I had a lot of guilt about that... I'm not doing anything here and I'm not at home with my mom." She says the song "talks about my mom, talks about... things I felt about my sister." On Zach Sang (S13, about 18:00-20:00) she adds that she felt "very responsible... for other people's jobs" and "I wish I could take a pain away." Fans know the mother line. Quoting the depression from that answer while dropping the guilt, the responsibility and the mother line presents the song as Four material when, by her account, it holds Two-leaning material too.
findings.acceptance_test: The article either (a) adds at most one clause, in her framing and with no medical update (per the research sensitivity note), saying that "Pure" was written while she felt guilty about being away from her ill mother, and weighs the mother-pain line alongside the sister and "real" lines in the Four/Two case; or (b) stops calling "Pure" the record's clearest Four evidence. Any lyric quoted is checked against the official lyric sheet, not captions.

findings.passage: But asked in March 2026 why she felt that way, she gave an answer that reads like a Two: she made herself needed.
findings.problem: The draft presents the Z100 answer as the explanation she gave for the visitor feeling. She has given at least one other, in the most-read profile in the record. In the Rolling Stone UK cover story (S01, May 2026) she ties the album's central idea to ADHD: "That's what a lot of the music is about, like 'The Visitor' – struggling to keep up with people and being [too] aware of everything, you end up losing people – and you're temporary." The same piece reports that at school she "would have always been regarded as popular, but says she slipped between friend groups, unable to settle" (writer's framing). To Notion (S04) she linked her childhood feelings to undiagnosed neurodivergence ("everyone would be like, 'You're so dramatic, you're so emotional, you're so sad!'"). The draft reduces all this to 'Rolling Stone UK reported an ADHD diagnosis.' It also leaves out that she began the Z100 answer with "Don't know." The detail of feeling like a visitor while seen as popular is missing too, and it is arguably the most type-relevant detail on the 4 vs 2 question: felt apartness in spite of acceptance, against actual exclusion.
findings.acceptance_test: The opening and the 'What the record can't separate yet' section say she has given more than one account of the visitor feeling: weight-based exclusion and making herself needed (Z100, March 2026), and ADHD, masking and losing track of people (Rolling Stone UK, May 2026). Each is attributed and dated as her own explanation, not the article's diagnosis, so 'Nothing here reads a type from her health' still holds. The intro no longer suggests the Z100 answer was her only or settled explanation. The 'regarded as popular but unsettled' detail is either used, attributed to Rolling Stone UK's framing, or deliberately left out with a reason in the resolution.

findings.passage: Her public record is about a year old and comes almost entirely from two promotional cycles
findings.problem: Informed readers will see this as inaccurate, and the draft says it three times (intro, the 60-word type answer, the type FAQ). Her breakthrough is a year old. Her public record is not. She began posting covers on TikTok in 2021 at 16, building a following partly through a viral "Redbone" cover (Wikipedia S31; Atwood S07). She said she found her manager "from posting one video" (Interview S03, March 2026). She released "Need Me" (May 24, 2024), "Maybe" (August 2024, UK No. 45, later certified), "Taxi Driver" and "Back to Blonde" (2024), and the EP Sink Now, Swim Later (February 2025). First-person interviews run from March 2025, about 19 months. The erased early career also takes context out of two parts of the article. (a) The 'nepo baby' paragraph says 'no response from her has been found' but leaves out her own documented route in, via TikTok and a manager found through one video. C29's alternative already records this. (b) The school-leaving story prints the producer's promise as drive and risk-taking. In the March 2026 Interview Q&A, which the draft cites elsewhere, she calls it dropping out "for honestly a bad reason" and "for quite a foolish reason," describes it as "false promises, older producer man," and calls herself "very stubborn and headstrong." Hey Alma (S26) repeats "foolish." A lead, not yet verified: a January 29, 2025 Melodic Magazine EP announcement (opened by this reviewer; not in the evidence record; speaker attribution unclear, perhaps an artist or label statement) frames the EP around "the desire to be needed and kept around" and "escaping through fantasy." If it can be attributed, it shows the 'needed' theme before the album campaign, which bears on 'the arc she tells... is also the arc of the album she was promoting.'
findings.acceptance_test: The intro, the type answer and the type FAQ describe the record's age accurately and consistently, for example 'her breakthrough is a year old and her interview record about a year and a half'. At least one dated, sourced sentence covers the 2021 TikTok start and the 2024 singles. The nepotism paragraph includes her on-record account of how she was found, attributed as her account, or the resolution explains why not. The school-leaving passage includes her own retrospective verdict ('foolish'/'false promises') or the resolution explains why it was left out. 'Need Me' and the Melodic statement appear only if an opened, attributable source supports what they are about. No speculation links the unnamed producer to anyone else.

findings.passage: She chased a style before settling on her own.
findings.problem: The most recognizable thing about her (the '60s beehive, cat-eye flicks and box dresses that every profile in the record opens with) never appears, though her own account of it bears directly on the Four-versus-Three question the article calls unresolved. To Rolling Stone UK (S01): "My hair felt like armour. It made me feel more myself, even though it looked less like me," and the look as "an elevated version of myself... made me feel really secure." She also said her earlier baggy streetwear was dictated by body issues and that "I hated the idea of people being able to see me and perceive me." To Interview (S03): "It took me a really long time to find my style because I grew up, honestly, hating my body." The Vevo quote is also stripped of context. Hey Alma's fuller version (S26) is time-bound and specific: "A challenge, I think, for the last year... I didn't think who I was, you know, what my identity was, was enough. So I kept trying to be cooler than I was. Like, a north-west London Jewish girl who sings jazz, you know?" She ends with going "back to why I started doing music." The draft splits it, places 'not enough' in the type section as a timeless heart-triad statement, files 'cooler' under the Three case, and drops both the identity she thought wasn't enough and how it resolved.
findings.acceptance_test: One short, sourced passage says what 'her own' style is and gives her explanation (the armour / 'more myself, even though it looked less like me' line, quoted exactly from Rolling Stone UK), and the Four/Three/Six weighing uses it. The Vevo quotation keeps its time frame ('for the last year'), is attributed as quoted by Hey Alma, and is not presented as a lifelong statement. The resolution says whether the 'north-west London Jewish girl who sings jazz' self-description is used.

findings.passage: "Lady in the Mirror" was about being bullied at school when
findings.problem: The hook keeps the validation detail (the room turning to look at her filming mother) and drops what she says the song was about. In the same NYLON piece (S05): "The song was about how the only person who really knows what's going on is me, the person in the mirror," a nod to Michael Jackson's "Man in the Mirror" (also in S37). She also says "I don't really know what possessed me to do that... It was kind of insane." For a profile whose leading read is Four, the first song's own subject (being misunderstood, with only herself as witness) is the more revealing formative detail, and leaving it out makes the opening read as approval-seeking alone.
findings.acceptance_test: The opening includes the 'person in the mirror' explanation from NYLON, quoted exactly, or the resolution gives a reason for leaving it out. Opening word count stays about the same.

findings.passage: On Genius: "I'm kind of jealous of my own imagination."
findings.problem: Placed straight after the New York story, the Genius line reads as being about the man who never came. It is from her "You Stole the Show" commentary (S24) and is about a different scene: an ex outside a venue, "one moment where it almost seemed like it could be real again." The draft calls longing for someone absent 'the most distinctive pattern in the record' but documents only one episode. The record has more. In March 2026 she told Interview (S03) that "You Stole the Show" (released July 2025, one of her best-known songs) "is about living it every night and just imagining what would happen if that person was there." To Lyrical Lemonade (S16) she said of pretending something is real, "I've had that so many different times."
findings.acceptance_test: The Genius quotation is attributed to the "You Stole the Show" commentary and to a different relationship. At least one dated sentence sets out the second instance ("You Stole the Show," 2025) so the 'most distinctive pattern' claim rests on repetition across songs and time, not on one story.

findings.passage: one framed around helping listeners feel less alone, Two
findings.problem: Open cases need settle signals that discriminate. This branch is already met by routine promotional talk, so it cannot. She has framed her music as helping listeners since at least November 2025: "To go through something myself, and to be able to create something that's helped me, and then help other people. It's the biggest gift that I have" (Notion, S04). In July 2026 on Z100 (S19) she said "I really hope there's a song in there for everyone... that is actually really normal and really okay." Almost every artist says this during a release, so hearing it about album two would not favor Two.
findings.acceptance_test: The second-album signal's Two branch names something not already routine in her interviews, such as a costly choice made for a specific person or collaborator, or a framing of the record as service at the expense of her own preference. Or the signal says her existing 'help other people' statements are on record and explains why they don't count. The settle-signal FAQ stays consistent with the body.

protected_passages.passage: Every day, she said, she walked down the stairs and imagined him outside the door, playing out "what I thought would happen if he was there."
protected_passages.reason: Matches the Zach Sang transcript (S13, about 46:00-47:00) and Lyrical Lemonade (S16, about 21:00). It is the most vivid, specific scene in the record, told without speculating about the unnamed man.

protected_passages.passage: And on a day she wasn't "feeling accomplished," she told Zach Sang, her "solution to that was wearing a suit" to the studio.
protected_passages.reason: A distinctive, verified detail (S13, about 27:00) that a fan would recognize. It brings in her self-mocking humor without flattering her.

protected_passages.passage: Even her signature method deflates the myth.
protected_passages.reason: Takes apart the one-take mystique that other profiles (Interview, Rolling Stone UK) repeat, using her own admission to the AP. A good example of the article refusing flattery.

protected_passages.passage: Melancholy and candor are her genre's currency. That doesn't make hers false. It makes them weak evidence of motive.
protected_passages.reason: A fair statement of the incentive problem behind the open case, backed by the manager's own 'honest' campaign framing. Short and memorable.

protected_passages.passage: "I have to do it," she said.
protected_passages.reason: Verified in S13 (about 21:00). She says the same to NYLON ('I have to make music... It's more than a want'), so the ending rests on a recurring self-description, not a one-off line.

assessment: Fan-proxy read. The draft resists flattery, handles the unnamed men and the nepotism framing carefully, and every quotation I rechecked against the research-stage transcripts and saved texts for S01, S03-S06, S13, S16-S22, S24, S26, S31, S36 and S37 is worded accurately. (These were the research stage's 2026-10-14 copies, not fresh fetches, except one new page, Melodic Magazine, January 29, 2025.) The problems are context and coverage, and one changes the argument. fan-01: the July 2026 'if you don't want me, don't have me' line and the 'completely opposed' line are her rejection of withdrawal, both told in the past tense, while she describes giving 'a lot of myself' in the present tense. The verdict's tense-based tie-breaker inverts its sources and appears again in the Two section, the Four case and the Type 2 FAQ. Fixing it may weaken or move the leading read. If the enneagram value changes, the standard's --refresh --expanded-review path applies. 'Pure' is used for Four evidence without the mother and guilt context that she puts first in the same answers (fan-02). Her ADHD explanation of the visitor feeling is reduced to a diagnosis mention (fan-03). Her 2021-2024 TikTok-to-EP career is erased by 'public record about a year old', which matters for the nepotism paragraph and the school-leaving story (fan-04). Her '60s look and her own 'armour' account of it, the clearest identity evidence for 4 vs 3, are missing (fan-05). Open-case eligibility still holds in my view: she is an adult, the breakthrough was in October 2025, and the pre-2025 TikTok material is mostly covers, so not a deep skipped record. The 'about a year old' wording still needs correcting. The similarity advisory did not trip (max 0.095 vs Freddie Mercury, a triad-vocabulary sentence), and comparing the actual arguments found no meaningful reuse. Risks: sensitive allegations (the unnamed older man and producer, nepotism labels, health and a family member's illness) and contested typing are both present. I found no historical source uncertainty, and the draft itself does not change the research thesis.
